finding.headline: At age 65, sign up for Medicare on time even if you keep working.
details: The Initial Enrollment Period lasts for 7 months, starting 3 months before you turn 65 and ending 3 months after that month.
If you miss it, you may have to wait to sign up and pay a monthly Part B late enrollment penalty as long as you have Part B.
Social Security benefits rise if you delay claiming beyond full retirement age; the increase stops at age 70.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $63,177 a year: $6,000 into a 401(k) or IRA, $3,000 from your employer's match, $54,177 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $50,100 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70, which pays about $62,100 a year.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 88. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
